Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette: Mr. Tran, a 74-year-old Vietnamese American welder, has lived with the haunting memories of his time in the war zone since he was young. Now married and settled in the United States for decades, Mr. Tran still vividly recalls the sounds of explosions and gunfire that filled the air during those tumultuous years. The auditory triggers from car horns and sirens evoke a visceral response, transporting him back to the chaos of that time. Mr. Tran’s story begins when he was just a young man in Vietnam, caught up in a war zone where daily life was fraught with danger. During one particularly harrowing event, Mr. Tran found himself amidst intense combat while trying to protect his family and community. The experience left him feeling overwhelmed by the chaos and violence surrounding him. Despite his best efforts to stay safe, he felt that his actions were inadequate in preventing harm. In the aftermath of those events, Mr. Tran emigrated to the United States with his wife, hoping for a quieter life away from the dangers of war. However, the memories continued to haunt him. The sound of car horns or sirens on his way to work would often trigger intense flashbacks and feelings of breathlessness. He started avoiding open spaces where he felt vulnerable, choosing instead to stay close to home whenever possible. Mr. Tran’s avoidance extended beyond just physical locations; he also avoided talking about the war with others, fearing that reliving those moments through conversation might cause him further distress. When his wife gently encouraged him to share more, Mr. Tran would redirect his thoughts by thinking of something else entirely—anything to keep the memories at bay. Over time, these avoidance behaviors began to affect his work as a welder. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on his tasks and often felt hypervigilant, constantly on guard for any signs of danger. This hyperalertness made it hard for him to relax or fall asleep at night, leading to sleepless nights and fatigue during the day. Mr. Tran’s memory of the war is fragmented; he feels as though parts are missing and that what remains seems alien and almost unbelievable. The memory of those extreme events is so intense that they sometimes feel like they happened to someone else rather than to him. This disjointedness makes it challenging for him to fully process or integrate his experiences. The injustice of the situation weighs heavily on Mr. Tran’s mind. He feels deeply wronged by what he experienced and believes that nothing has been done to address the injustices. The lack of accountability from those responsible further compounds his feelings of self-blame, as if he could have prevented some of the suffering through different actions. Mr. Tran’s relationship with his wife has also been strained due to his reluctance to share his experiences. She notices a change in him but struggles to understand what he is going through without him opening up. The cumulative effect of these symptoms and behaviors has led Mr. Tran to seek help, hoping that someone can assist him in making sense of his past and finding some peace. What frightens Mr. Tran the most is the possibility of reliving those traumatic memories and the uncertainty about how he will cope with them in the future. He hopes that by talking to a therapist, he might be able to find ways to manage his symptoms better and perhaps even reconnect with his wife on a deeper level. His ultimate hope is to regain some sense of control over his life and to live without the constant fear and hypervigilance that have plagued him for so long.
